passage:
Lalit walked home along the canal path with Chetan after the evening class at the town institute. It was the accounts course, twice a week, and Lalit had done six months of it and disliked every session.

"Six months gone," said Chetan. "If you leave now, all that is wasted."

Lalit kicked a stone. "That's the wrong question. Those six months are gone whether I stay or not. The question is the next six." He counted on his fingers. "Six more months, Tuesdays and Saturdays, four hours each. Would I rather spend those on this, or on the drawing class that starts in June?"

He was quiet for a minute. "The drawing class. I keep what I learned about spreadsheets. I don't need the certificate."

qa.q: How many months of the course had Lalit already done?
qa.a: Lalit had done six months of the course.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the accounts course?
qa.a: Lalit disliked every session and was reluctant to spend more time on it.

qa.q: What could Lalit do before leaving the course?
qa.a: Lalit could talk with the institute and family, and check whether part of the course can be kept, so that the decision rests on facts about what lies ahead.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Lalit's reasoning?
qa.a: Chetan may feel surprised, having thought that leaving meant wasting the six months, and may be persuaded by the new question.

grounding: Shows a student asking whether the next six months are worth it instead of whether the first six were wasted.

passage: In a flat in Montevideo, Santiago sat at the piano his parents had rented six months ago and stared at the sheet of scales. He hated it. Every Tuesday lesson with Marek felt like an hour of fog. That evening he did something new. He took a notebook and wrote two questions. The first: "Did I waste six months?" He crossed it out. That one didn't matter; those months were gone either way. The second: "Do I want the next six months of this?" He thought about Tuesday afternoons, about the scales, about the guitar in his cousin's room that he actually picked up every time he visited. The answer was no. He showed his parents the notebook and asked if he could finish the month and then switch to guitar.

qa.q: What was the second question Santiago wrote?
qa.a: "Do I want the next six months of this?"

qa.q: Why did Santiago cross out the first question?
qa.a: He realised those six months were gone either way; he felt calmer focusing on what lay ahead rather than guilty about the past.

qa.q: What would you advise Santiago to discuss with his parents?
qa.a: How to finish the month properly and how to try guitar for a set time, so the switch is planned, not a whim.

qa.q: How might Marek see Santiago's decision?
qa.a: Marek might be disappointed but may also respect that Santiago thought it through and is finishing the month.

grounding: A student who dislikes a course he has done for six months asks whether the next six are worth it, not whether the first six were wasted.

passage: At the sports academy's counselling room, Tushar sat opposite Payal Ma'am, the counsellor, twisting his cap. He had done six months of the cricket fast-bowling programme and dreaded every session. "I feel like if I quit now, everything I did is wasted," he said. Payal Ma'am didn't argue. She just asked, "If you'd never started, would you join the next six months today?" He was quiet for a long time. He thought about his aching back, the dread before practice, and the chess club he kept looking at through the window. "No," he said slowly. "The six months already happened. They're not coming back whether I stay or go." Payal Ma'am nodded. "Then let's talk to your parents about the next step together."

What was Tushar feeling when he twisted his cap?
qa.a: He felt anxious and torn, dreading the sessions but afraid quitting would waste everything.

qa.q: What else could Tushar try before fully switching to chess?
qa.a: Visit the chess club for a few sessions while finishing any commitments, and talk it through with his parents and the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Tushar's parents see the change?
qa.a: They may worry about the time already spent, but a calm talk with the counsellor could help them see he's choosing the future, not running away.

grounding: A student six months into a course he dislikes asks whether the next six months are worth it, not whether the first six were wasted.
